questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presented with 3 days of whitishyellow urethral discharge. He reported that the discharge was staining his underwear. He also reported pain with urination. He had unprotected vaginal intercourse approximately1 week ago. On examination, there was white discharge at the meatus. There were no genital lesions and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Microscopy:
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM stat and azithromycin 1 gram stat
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat and azithromycin 1 gram stat

questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat and azithromycin 1 gram stat Gonococcal urethritis can be reliably diagnosed via Gram stain performed on samples obtained in office. The presence of gram-negative diplococci in the setting of neutrophils is highly suggestive of gonococcal urethritis. Ceftriaxone 250 mg plus azithromycin 1 g is the recommended regimen for uncomplicated urethritis, cervicitis, and proctitis. NAAT tests should be sent on this patient, but treatment should not be delayed until results return. Ceftriaxone 125 mg intramuscularly was used to treat gonorrhea in the past but is no longer recommended. The higher dose of ceftriaxone plus the addition of azithromycin is recommended to reduce the development of resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones were recommended for the treatment of gonorrhea in the past, but because of high rates of resistance, their use is no longer recommended. (Image from Braverman PK. Urethritis, vulvovaginitis, and cervicitis. In Long SS, Prober CG, Fischer M, eds. Principles and Practice of Pediatric Infectious Diseases. 5th ed. Elsevier; 2018.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q23

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presented with a swollen, painful, and erythematous right wrist of 1-week duration. His symptoms were associated with fever, chills, and generalized malaise. Upon review of systems, he recounted painless urethral discharge in the weeks prior to his presentation. He was sexually active and reported unprotected vaginal intercourse with 3 casual partners in the last 6 months. On examination his temperature was 100.7°F (38.2°C). His right wrist was erythematous with a small effusion and tenderness to palpation along the insertion of the tendon. There were three small vesiculopustular lesions overlying the right thenar eminence. Investigations: Total white cell count 12,800/mL Two sets of peripheral blood cultures negative X-ray of the joint did not demonstrate a fracture or erosion of the underlying bone Joint fluid: Macroscopic appearances: turbid synovial fluid Microscopy: leukocyte count 42,000 cells mm 3, 78% neutrophils No organisms seen on Gram stain. No crystals seen
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone IV and azithromycin PO The patient is a young sexually active male with gonococcal arthritis with concern for disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) with associated purulent arthritis given systemic symptoms, tenosynovitis, and vesiculopustular lesions noted on physical exam. With this entity, distal joints are commonly affected (knees, ankles, wrists). Lyme arthritis, while often monoarticular, tends to affect larger joints, such as the knee. He is young for a crystal arthropathy; and while staphylococcal arthritis must be considered, he is unlikely to have an MRSA joint infection, and ceftriaxone would safely cover an MSSA infection. Patients with DGI may have evidence of asymptomatic infection at other sites (oropharynx, genitourinary, or rectal) and testing from these sites is recommended. Cultures obtained may or may not be positive. Gonorrhea and chlamydia nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) from urogenital and extragenital sites can be sent in order for indirect confirmation of infection. Some laboratories may offer NAAT testing of synovial fluid. Initial therapy recommended is dual antibiotic therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone daily for at least 1 week in addition to a one-time dose of azithromycin given increasing rates of resistance.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q15

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man attended for routine follow up. He was asymptomatic. He was known to have HIV and was taking a fixed-dose regimen of abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine He was last screened for STI 6 months previously. He was sexually active, and reported three casual male partners in the previous 3 months. He reported that he discloses his HIV status to partners. He engaged in anal receptive and oral insertive and receptive sex. He used condoms for anal sex most of the time. On examination, his oropharynx was clear. His urogenital examination was without discharge, lymphadenopathy, or unusual skin findings. Rectal examination was performed, and no abnormalities were noted. Investigations: CD4 count 900 cells/mm3 HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What screening tests should be performed?

options.text: No screening is recommended at today’s visit. Screen annually
Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis plus syphilis serology
Urine screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis

questions.explanation: Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology This patient has high risk for exposure to STI. In this case, STI screening is recommended at 3- or 6-month intervals. Screen urethral (urine) and rectal sites by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis . Oropharyngeal screening for C. trachomatis is not recommended. NAAT or culture can be used for oropharyngeal screening for N. gonorrhoeae. Note that some NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae are less sensitive because they cross react with other Neisseria spp. found in the oral environment.

questions.question: A man returns to clinic for recurrent mucopurulent urethritis. He was initially seen a few days ago and was started on appropriate antimicrobial therapy. You suspect Neisseria gonorrhea.

parts.text: What specimen would you send and what test would you ask for?
What is the most common mechanism of resistance to 3rd generation cephalosporins in N. gonorrhea?

cohort_answer.text: Cefixime resistance is caused by an alteration in PBP conferred by a mutation in the penA gene of PBP2. A single locus mutation can confer resistance to cefixime with an increase in ceftriaxone MIC. But full ceftriaxone resistance usually requires mutations in several loci, which is why cefixime becomes resistant before ceftriaxone.

questions.question: Practical station: Blood culture with GNDC on smear. Growth on chocolate. API with sugars: glucose positive, maltose negative, sucrose negative.

parts.text: Name organism.
What are 3 selective components of Thayer-Martin media

questions.model_answer: a) Organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus, oxidase-positive, grows on chocolate agar, ferments glucose only - not maltose/sucrose/lactose, distinguishing from N. meningitidis which ferments both glucose and maltose). b) Selective components of modified Thayer-Martin media (3): vancomycin (inhibits gram-positives), colistin (inhibits gram-negative bacilli), nystatin (inhibits yeast/fungi); trimethoprim also included to inhibit swarming Proteus.

questions.question: 12. 25 year old male with gonococcal urethritis. The culture reveals a N. gonorrhoeae with reduced susceptibility (MIC > 0,5) to cefixime, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone. The patient had a severe anaphylactic reaction to penicillin in the past.

parts.text: List 2 therapeutic regimen available in Canada for this particular scenario (drug – dose – route of administration).
b) List 3 important mechanisms of resistance of N. gonorrhoeae to B-lactam antibiotics.
c) Why is the susceptibility decreased for cefixime, but unaffected for Ceftriaxone?

cohort_answer.text: PHAC regimens: Ctx 250mg IM x1 + 1g po azithro x1; Azithromycin 2g PO x1 + Gent 240mg IM x1; Doxy 100mg x7 days + Gent 240mg IM x1; Azithro 2g po x1 + cipro 500mg po x1; Azithromycin 2g PO x1 monotherapy (should not be used as monotherapy unless cephalosporins are contraindicated, as resistance has been reported). Mechanisms of resistance: Beta-lactamases (hydrolysis of beta-lactam ring); Altered target binding site (PBPs); Efflux pump (MDR). Cefixime vs Ceftriaxone: Cefixime resistance is caused by an alteration in PBP conferred by a mutation in the penA gene of PBP2. A single locus mutation can confer resistance to cefixime with an increase in ceftriaxone MIC, but full ceftriaxone resistance usually requires mutations in several loci, which is why cefixime becomes resistant before ceftriaxone.

questions.question: 3 day old neonate, mother had no prenatal care - 17yo and street-associated, left hospital already. Baby has bilateral chemosis and purulent discharge from eyes.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen?
What are three neonatal disease presentations of this pathogen
What are three microbiologic tests to assess for complications or verify diagnosis
If this was limited to conjunctivitis what is the therapy?
If the mother is found what treatment does she need? Drug, dose, duration

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely pathogen: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (ophthalmia neonatorum, onset day 2-5 of life, hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis). b) Three neonatal presentations: (1) Ophthalmia neonatorum/conjunctivitis. (2) Disseminated infection (bacteremia, arthritis, sepsis). (3) Scalp abscess (from fetal scalp electrode) - also rhinitis and anorectal infection acceptable. c) Microbiologic tests (3): (1) Gram stain of conjunctival exudate (gram-negative intracellular diplococci). (2) Culture on chocolate/Thayer-Martin media with confirmatory biochemical/NAAT testing. (3) Blood culture ± CSF/joint fluid culture to rule out disseminated disease. d) Conjunctivitis-only therapy: single dose ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM (max 250 mg), plus saline eye irrigation; also treat for possible concurrent chlamydia. e) Maternal treatment if found: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 dose (gonorrhea) PLUS azithromycin 1 g PO x1 dose (empiric chlamydia co-treatment).

questions.question: [Afternoon session] Male with gonococcal urethritis. Isolate has reduced susceptibility to cefixime but remains susceptible to ceftriaxone. Has anaphylactic reaction to penicillin.

parts.text: Name 2 treatment regimens available in Canada.
Name three mechanisms of resistance of N. meningitidis to beta-lactams
Why does ceftriaxone remain susceptible while cefixime has lost its effect?

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Gentamicin 240mg IM single dose + azithromycin 2g PO single dose; Gentamicin 240mg IM + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days; Azithromycin + ciprofloxacin (PHAC Guidelines; test of cure needed). Resistance mechanisms: Beta-lactamases (BlaTEM-1, plasmid); altered PBP2a (penA); porin alterations (penB); efflux pump (mtr). cohort_answer.text: N. gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250mg IM + 1g Azithromycin. C. trachomatis - azithromycin 1g PO or doxy 100mg PO BID x7d. parts.text: Man with gonococcal pharyngitis, what is the treatment (be specific, dose, duration).

questions.model_answer: a) Gonococcal pharyngitis: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (dual therapy; test of cure recommended given lower cephalosporin efficacy at pharyngeal site). b) Disseminated gonococcal infection with endocarditis: ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV daily for a prolonged course - endocarditis requires 4 weeks IV therapy (vs 7 days for uncomplicated DGI/septic arthritis), plus azithromycin 1 g PO x1 for chlamydia coverage. c) [insufficient stem detail to answer]. d) Cervicitis with cephalosporin anaphylaxis: azithromycin 2 g PO single dose (alternative regimen when cephalosporins contraindicated), ideally with infectious disease/culture-guided susceptibility given resistance concerns; gentamicin 240 mg IM x1 plus azithromycin 2 g PO x1 is another PHAC-endorsed alternative. e) Causes of non-gonococcal urethritis (4): Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis (also HSV, adenovirus). f) Situations requiring test of cure (4): (1) Pharyngeal gonorrhea. cohort_answer.text: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose; Azithromycin 2g PO + Gentamicin 240mg IM (if severe penicillin or cephalosporin allergy). questions.question: A patient receiving eculizumab presents with fever, pustular rash, and right knee swelling/pain.

parts.text: What arm of the immune system does eculizumab affect?
What TWO organisms are the most likely cause of her presentation?
What is the first-line treatment for both organisms above?
List TWO vaccines that should be administered in patients starting eculizumab (no brand names).

questions.model_answer:
a) Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody against complement C5 that blocks the terminal complement pathway (prevents formation of the C5b-9 membrane attack complex).
b) Two most likely organisms: Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (this presentation - fever, pustular rash, and monoarticular arthritis - is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection, and both Neisseria species are markedly more virulent when terminal complement is blocked).
c) First-line treatment for both organisms: ceftriaxone.
d) Two vaccines that should be given before/when starting eculizumab: meningococcal conjugate vaccine (serogroups A, C, W, Y) and meningococcal serogroup B vaccine.
questions.beyond_mandell: Disseminated gonococcal infection triad and vaccine timing recommendations for eculizumab are general clinical/CDC knowledge complementing the Mandell complement-deficiency discussion.

questions.question: Name the first-line treatment regimen for the following infections in men who have sex with men, as per the Public Health Agency of Canada.

parts.text: Neisseria gonorrhoea
Chlamydia trachomatis
Mycoplasma genitalium

questions.model_answer: PHAC first-line MSM STI regimens: (1) N. gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (dual therapy, especially given pharyngeal involvement common in MSM). (2) C. trachomatis - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days (preferred over azithromycin for rectal chlamydia, common in MSM). (3) Mycoplasma genitalium - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days followed by azithromycin 1 g PO then 500 mg daily x3 days (if macrolide-susceptible), or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily x7-14 days if resistance/failure. (4) Trichomonas vaginalis - metronidazole 2 g PO single dose. (5) Ureaplasma urealyticum - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days.

questions.question: You see a 25 year-old man presenting with right knee and ankle septic arthritis. Blood cultures are positive for a gram negative diplococcus.

parts.text: What is the most likely organism?
List THREE other tests that should be performed.
List THREE host-factors that predispose to disseminated infection with this organism.

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (disseminated gonococcal infection). b) Three other tests: (1) Synovial fluid gram stain, culture, and NAAT. (2) NAAT of urethral/cervical, pharyngeal, and rectal sites (mucosal screening, higher yield than blood culture). (3) HIV and other STI screening (syphilis, chlamydia) given risk behaviors. c) Host factors predisposing to disseminated gonococcal infection (3): (1) Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9). (2) Female sex, particularly menstruation or pregnancy. (3) Systemic lupus erythematosus/other conditions causing functional complement deficiency; also asymptomatic mucosal infection allowing prolonged exposure.

questions.question: You are seeing a patient with disseminated gonorrhoea.

parts.text: What is the MOST common manifestation of disseminated gonorrhoea?
What are THREE other extragenital manifestations of gonorrhoea (do not include disseminated)
Based on the Canadian STI treatment guidelines, what is the standard therapy for uncomplicated pharyngeal gonorrhoea?

questions.model_answer: a) Most common manifestation of disseminated gonorrhea: dermatitis-arthritis (tenosynovitis) syndrome - migratory polyarthralgia with tenosynovitis and scattered pustular/hemorrhagic skin lesions. b) Three other extragenital manifestations (excluding disseminated disease): (1) Pharyngitis. (2) Conjunctivitis. (3) Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome); proctitis also acceptable. c) Standard therapy for uncomplicated pharyngeal gonorrhea (Canadian STI guidelines): ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose, with test of cure recommended.

questions.question: Please complete the following table regarding mechanisms of resistance

parts.text: Complete the table (Organism / Antibiotic / Mechanism / Gene associated) for: Enterobacter cloacae (Ceftazidime), MRSA (Daptomycin), Neisseria gonorrhea (Ceftriaxone)

questions.model_answer:
Enterobacter cloacae / Ceftazidime: Mechanism - derepressed hyperproduction of chromosomal AmpC cephalosporinase; Gene - ampC (chromosomal, with regulatory ampR/ampD mutations).
MRSA / Daptomycin: Mechanism - cell membrane remodeling that increases positive surface charge and repels the cationic lipopeptide, plus membrane thickening reducing drug penetration; Gene - mprF (and yycFG/walKR system mutations).
Neisseria gonorrhoeae / Ceftriaxone: Mechanism - altered penicillin-binding protein 2 with reduced cephalosporin affinity, compounded by efflux pump overexpression and porin loss; Gene - penA (mosaic PBP2), with contributions from mtrR and penB.
questions.beyond_mandell: Resistance mechanism/gene detail is general clinical microbiology knowledge, not specific to this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: 17 year-old boy returning from Thailand with tenosynovitis, arthritis, and pustules.

parts.text: Diagnosis
Treatment
Emerging resistance pattern
Mechanism of resistance

cohort_answer.text: Disseminated gonococcal infection. Treatment: Ceftriaxone 2g IV/IM x7 days; Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. Resistance patterns: Tetracyclines - 23% resistance rate in USA; rising FQ resistance 2000-2006 led to removal from first-line in 2007, 39% resistance in Canada by 2015; increase in strains with elevated MIC to cefixime/ceftriaxone 2000-2010 (CLSI elevated MIC 0.5; cefixime MIC>0.25 went 0.2%->1.4%; ceftriaxone MIC>0.125 went 0.1%->0.3%); high level ceftriaxone resistance first seen 2009 Japan (MIC=2); global spread of ceftriaxone-resistant FC428 clone (MIC 0.5-1) in Denmark, Canada, Australia (penA mosaic); azithromycin elevated MIC 0.125-0.5 associated with treatment failure of 1g dose, high level resistance (MIC>256) first detected 2004 Scotland; XDR gonorrhea (CTX MIC 0.5, azithro MIC>256) - Feb-March 2018 one case UK, 2 cases Australia, links to SE Asia; UK case treated with ceftriaxone+spectinomycin, test of cure positive, susceptible to spectinomycin/gentamicin (MIC 2)/ertapenem (MIC 0.032), cured with 3-day ertapenem course. Mechanisms of resistance: Penicillin - penicillinase; Tetracyclines; FQ - gyrA, gyrB, parC mutations (altered target, CDC removed FQ first-line recommendation in 2007 due to 13% resistance); Cephalosporins - penA (altered PBP2, mosaic mutations), ponA (altered PBP1), Mtr efflux pump increased activity, penB (PorB1b porin loss); Azithromycin - efflux, mutations in 23S rRNA erm methylase gene (altered target).

questions.question: Patient with N. gonorrhoeae urethritis. Resistant to cipro. Resistant to Cefixime. Sensitive to Ceftriaxone. Hives/anaphylaxis with previous dose of cefixime.

parts.text: Give 2 possible treatments, including dose

cohort_answer.text: Gentamicin 240mg IM + Azithromycin 2g PO x1 dose. Alternatively Gentamicin 240mg IM + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days unless documented tetracycline resistance. If pushed: Azithro 2g PO x1 + cipro 500mg x1 if known FQ sensitivity or good local antibiogram + test of cure feasible

questions.question: List of various STIs - what investigations (if any) are indicated, and first line tx option for each?

parts.text: A) Patient who has had orogenital intercourse with patient positive for gonorrhea

cohort_answer.text: Depends on who did what and put what where. Throat, urethral and rectal swab for gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT +/- cultures (based on local lab validation). Treat with Ceftriaxone IM + azithromycin. Test of cure from all positive sites

questions.question: Preferred therapy

parts.text: A) Gonococcal urethritis in pen allergic patient

cohort_answer.text: Would assess nature of the allergy. Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + azithromycin 1g PO x1 if non-severe reaction. Azithromycin 2g PO x1 + gentamicin 240mg IM x1 (or gent IV) if severe reaction. Azithromycin 2g PO alone is the least preferred alternative therapy

questions.question: Q38 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Pt with N. gonorrhea urethritis. Resistant to Cipro, resistant to cefixime. Sensitive to Ceftriaxone. Hives/anaphylaxis with previous dose of cefixime.

parts.text: a) 3 mechanisms of resistance in gonorrhea
b) Explain why cefixime has high MIC, but ceftriaxone can still be sensitive
c) Give 2 possible treatments, including dose

cohort_answer.text: a) Antimicrobial destruction/modification by enzymes; target modification/protection reducing affinity; decreased influx; increased efflux. Specific: Gyrase & topoisomerase chromosomal mutations (gyrA/gyrB/parC/parE) - FQ resistance; tetM on conjugated plasmid - tetracycline resistance; penA (modifies PBP affinity) & penB (alters porin entry) - penicillin/beta-lactam resistance; mtr mutations - increased efflux. b) Ceftriaxone has longer C3 side chain, slightly different PBP binding sites; higher levels achieved with CTX (IM) vs cefixime (PO). c) If true IgE-mediated PCN allergy, avoid ceftriaxone: 1) Gentamicin 240mg IM x1 + azithromycin 2g PO x1. 2) Gentamicin 240mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days. 3) Desensitization to ceftriaxone, then ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + azithromycin 1g PO x1. Test of cure recommended if second line agent used or select situations (poor compliance, pregnancy, pharyngeal disease).

questions.question: Case of a rather hefty woman who developed migratory arthralgias and an image which showed a pustular rash. Gram stain with bean-shaped gram negative diplococci. Stated that she never left Montreal. On alternate version, showed a GNB.

parts.text: One epidemiological question that would be most important?
Dx?
Rx?
Why would you want to contact the lab if you suspect his Dx?

cohort_answer.text: Epi question: Sexual history. Dx: Disseminated gonococcal infection. Rx: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h x7 days, Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. Contact lab: requires special culture medium ('New York City' or 'Martin-Lewis') to improve culture yield; can also request NAAT on sterile fluid

questions.question: Q57 (2007). 17M returning from Thailand with tenosynovitis, arthritis, pustules.

parts.text: A) Diagnosis?
B) Treatment?
C) Emerging resistance pattern?
D) Mechanism of resistance?

cohort_answer.text: A) Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI). B) Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily x7 days AND Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. C) Ceftriaxone resistant (3.5%). D) penA (altered PBP); ponA (altered PBP1); Mtr efflux pump; PenB porin loss.

questions.question: 25 yo woman (Peds was 7 year old) on eculizumab for aHUS. Presents with 1 wk fever, pustular rash, swollen knee.

parts.text: What arm of immune system involved (0.5)
Name two most likely pathogens causing this presentation (1)
Name the empiric antibiotic to treat these two pathogens (0.5)
Name 2 vaccines indicated prior to starting eculizumab (no brand names) (1)

cohort_answer.text: Arm of immune system: Terminal complement pathway - blocking activation of complement protein C5. Pathogens: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; Neisseria meningitidis. Empiric antibiotic: Ceftriaxone. Vaccines: Meningococcal B and ACWY

questions.question: 26-year-old guy with sepsis and swollen painful knee, has a blood culture positive for gram negative diplococci (doesn't mention sexual history).

parts.text: What is the most likely organism (genus/species)
What three other microbiologic tests should you order
What are 3 host factors for dissemination?

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Other tests: HIV p24 Ag/Ab; Syphilis screen (EIA, RPR, TPPA); Urine NAAT for C. trachomatis. Host factors for dissemination: Recent menstruation; Pregnancy or the immediate postpartum state; Congenital or acquired complement deficiencies (C5-C8); Eculizumab; SLE (conflicting reports)

questions.question: You are consulted on a 15yo teenage boy who returned from a trip to Eastern Europe 3 weeks ago. During that trip he had a 3-day history of mild viral symptoms (fever, myalgias) that resolved. He also had unprotected sexual intercourse with a partner 6 months ago. He now has testicular pain and you note evidence of orchitis and epididymitis on exam. He also has submandibular tenderness without a mass on exam.

parts.text: Name 2 microbiologic tests that would confirm the diagnosis

cohort_answer.text: Likely diagnosis mumps; confirmatory tests: N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis urine NAAT (to rule out other causes of orchitis/epididymitis)

questions.question: Based on PHAC guidelines, name the recommended first-line treatment for the following for the MSM community (drug, dose, route, duration).

parts.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Chlamydia trachomatis
Trichomonas vaginalis
Mycoplasma genitalium
Ureaplasma urealyticum

cohort_answer.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM once PLUS Azithromycin 1g PO once. Chlamydia trachomatis: Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7 days (for LGV treat 21d). Trichomonas vaginalis: Metronidazole 2g PO once. Mycoplasma genitalium: Azithromycin 500mg PO day 1 followed by 250mg PO for total of 5d. Ureaplasma urealyticum: Doxycycline 100mg PO bid x7 days

questions.question: Q70 2023 Day 1. Gonorrhea Test of Cure (ToC) (2 or 4). (HIV/STI)

parts.text: Gonorrhea Test of Cure (2 or 4)

questions.model_answer: Test of cure for gonorrhea is recommended at all pharyngeal infection sites and in specific situations regardless of site: pregnancy, persistent symptoms after treatment, and use of an alternative (non-ceftriaxone-based) regimen - four key indications overall (pharyngeal site, pregnancy, symptom persistence, non-recommended regimen used).
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC Canadian Guidelines on Sexually Transmitted Infections

questions.question: 4 day old baby presenting with profuse purulent bilateral discharge of the eyes that started at day 3. Mother is 17 year old street youth with a history of IVDU who left the hospital AMA after delivery.

parts.text: What is the likely organism
Name 6 neonatal presentation of this disease
Name 3 microbiological tests for the diagnosis and testing for potential complications
Assuming it is only in conjunctivitis, what is the appropriate treatment for this patient (Drug, dose and length)
If you find the mother, what two drugs do you give empirically to the mother (drug, dose and length)

questions.model_answer: a) Likely organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. b) Neonatal presentations (6): (1) Ophthalmia neonatorum. (2) Disseminated gonococcal infection/bacteremia. (3) Arthritis. (4) Sepsis/meningitis. (5) Scalp abscess (fetal monitor site). (6) Rhinitis/anorectal or vaginal infection. c) Microbiologic tests (3): (1) Gram stain of ocular discharge (intracellular gram-negative diplococci). (2) Culture on chocolate/modified Thayer-Martin media. (3) Blood culture (and CSF if signs of sepsis) to exclude dissemination. d) Conjunctivitis-only treatment: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg) plus saline eye irrigation. e) Empiric maternal treatment (2 drugs): ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 (gonorrhea) plus azithromycin 1 g PO x1 (chlamydia coverage).

questions.question: Neonatal conjunctivitis differential based on timing/presentation.

parts.text: Bilateral/rapid onset/purulent presentation, usually pus wipes out and comes right back - what is this?
Unilateral or bilateral, usually 5 to 14 days after delivery - what is this?
Diagnostic test

cohort_answer.text: Rapid bilateral purulent conjunctivitis (pus recurs immediately after wiping) = gonococcal conjunctivitis. Onset 5-14 days after delivery = C. trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by lab testing: Gram stain and culture (chocolate agar and Thayer-Martin media for gonorrhea, blood agar for other organisms); Giemsa stain for chlamydial suspicion, though NAAT now more commonly used (less expensive, less labor than viral culture). Newborns with suspected C. trachomatis infection should have samples drawn from both conjunctivae and oropharynx; swabs should include conjunctival epithelial cells since C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism.

questions.question: Purulent conjunctivitis in a neonate whose mother is street involved.

parts.text: What are 3 samples to send for diagnosis and to identify potential complications?
What are 3 other neonatal sites of infection to be concerned about?
What agent to treat a neonate with?
What are two regimens to treat mother with?

questions.model_answer: a) Three samples for diagnosis/complications: (1) Conjunctival swab for Gram stain and culture (chocolate/Thayer-Martin media) plus NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. (2) Blood culture (assess for disseminated gonococcal infection/sepsis). (3) CSF analysis/culture if signs of sepsis or meningitis present. b) Three other neonatal sites of concern: disseminated infection/bacteremia, septic arthritis, and scalp abscess (from fetal monitor electrode site); rhinitis also acceptable. c) Neonatal treatment: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg), with saline eye irrigation. d) Two maternal treatment regimens: (1) Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose (gonorrhea) plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (chlamydia coverage). (2) If cephalosporin-allergic, azithromycin 2 g PO single dose (alternative gonorrhea regimen).

questions.question: Neonate with bilateral purulent conjunctivitis 3d after birth. Mom has RF for STI.

parts.text: Name causative pathogen genus and spp
Diagnosis (2-3 tests)
Therapy

questions.model_answer: a) Causative pathogen (genus/species): Neisseria gonorrhoeae (hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis presenting within the first few days of life is classic for gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, versus chlamydial which typically presents 5-14 days after birth). b) Diagnosis (2-3 tests): Gram stain of conjunctival exudate (intracellular gram-negative diplococci), culture on chocolate/Thayer-Martin selective media, and NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae (and co-testing for C. trachomatis). c) Therapy: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg) with saline eye irrigation; treat mother (and partner) empirically as well.

questions.question: A baby is born to a young mother who is living on the street, and who abandons her child in hospital so no further history is available. The baby develops bilateral purulent conjunctivitis.

parts.text: What is the most likely causative organism, to the genus and species?
What are three other neonatal manifestations of infection with this organism?
What are three microbiologic investigations that you would like to do for the baby?
What would be your recommended treatment, assuming that conjunctivitis is the only site involved?
What 2 empiric treatments would you recommend for the mother, if she returns?

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. b) Other neonatal manifestations (3): disseminated infection/bacteremia, septic arthritis, scalp abscess (also rhinitis, sepsis). c) Microbiologic investigations (3): Gram stain of eye discharge, culture on chocolate/Thayer-Martin selective media, blood culture to assess for dissemination. d) Treatment if conjunctivitis only: ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg IV/IM single dose (max 250 mg) with saline irrigation. e) Empiric maternal treatment (2 drugs): ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 plus azithromycin 1 g PO x1.

questions.question: 27-year old man with chlamydia, gonorrhea and treponemal test positive. His RPR is 1:256, w (NOTE: did not specify location of Chlamydia/gonorrhea infection, or whether patient is MSM etc) per PHAC

parts.text: What 3 drugs would you treat with? Include dose, route, duration
What are 2 reasons for RPR not decreasing 4 fold at 12 months, other than incorrect clinical staging at diagnosis

questions.model_answer:
a) 3 drugs with dose/route/duration: (1) benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1 dose for syphilis (assuming early syphilis given the high titer); (2) ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 dose for gonorrhea; (3) doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days for chlamydia.
b) 2 reasons RPR fails to decline 4-fold by 12 months (other than incorrect staging): (1) HIV coinfection, which can blunt/delay the serologic response to treatment; (2) reinfection with a new syphilis exposure during the follow-up period.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC Canadian Guidelines on Sexually Transmitted Infections for treatment doses.

questions.question: Q69 (2023 Day 1). 27 year old male with RPR 1:128 (negative RPR 3 months ago), positive chlamydia and gonorrhea. No specific symptoms mentioned. (HIV/STI)

parts.text: List 3 antibiotics indicated including name, dose, route, and frequency
If RPR not 4 fold decrease give 2 reasons why

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis: Early (Primary, Secondary, early latent) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1. Late (Late latent, tertiary) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly x3. Neurosyphilis - Crystalline Pen G 4 million units q4h IV x14 days.
Chlamydia: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days.
Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1.
If RPR not 4-fold decrease, 2 reasons: Recurrent infection; Neurosyphilis; Inadequate treatment.
